body_md: For each finite resistance $\beta$, the far-field limit $R\to\infty$ in~\eqref{eq:delay} is taken first to define $\tau_\beta$; Theorem~\ref{thm:large-beta} then describes its behavior as $\beta\to\infty$. title: Remark
body_md: In the deterministic additive-selection model of~\cite{PB1997}, the barrier strength is $B=[p]/p_x$; after scaling, this gives the resistance in~\eqref{eq:interface}. Their Appendix~A estimates establishment at the barrier from linearized growth. The numerical delay in their Figure~1A is computed from the difference in total allele numbers between solutions with and without a barrier after the wave has crossed, while Figure~1B follows the evolving difference in wave position. Definition~\eqref{eq:delay} instead specifies a limit of distant first-arrival times; Theorem~\ref{thm:phase} identifies this limit with the asymptotic phase difference divided by the wave speed.

title: Proof
body_md:
Extend $f$ to a globally Lipschitz function on $\mathbb R$. The contraction property of the linear semigroup makes the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:mild} a contraction on bounded measurable functions on a sufficiently short time interval. This gives local existence and uniqueness without requiring continuity of the initial data.

To obtain comparison, choose a Lipschitz constant $L$ for the extension, so that $s\mapsto f(s)+Ls$ is nondecreasing. In the equivalent integral formulation with the damped kernel $e^{-Lt}P_\beta(t,x,y)$ and reaction $f(u)+Lu$, positivity of the kernel and Picard iteration preserve the order of the initial data. Comparison with the constant solutions $0$ and $1$ gives $0\le u^\beta\le1$, and hence global continuation and independence of the chosen extension of $f$.

Kernel smoothing, followed by parabolic regularity for the folded Neumann
and Robin problems, gives positive-time classical regularity and the
transmission traces; see~\cite{Lieberman1996} for the scalar boundary
regularity tools. The explicit kernel supplies the interface structure used here. Finally, the kernel has the initial approximation property locally in $L^p$ and at continuity points away from the interface, while the reaction integral in \eqref{eq:mild} is $O(t)$ in $L^\infty$. This proves the asserted initial convergence.

label: lem:reflection-comparison
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define
\[
 c_\beta(t,x)=\int_0^1 f'\!\left(q_\beta(t,x)
 +s\bigl(p_\beta(t,x)-q_\beta(t,x)\bigr)\right)\,ds.
\]
Then $(D_\beta)_t=(D_\beta)_{xx}+c_\beta D_\beta$, with
$|c_\beta|\le\|f'\|_{L^\infty([0,1])}$ and
$D_\beta(0,x)=u_0(-x)/2\ge0$ not identically zero. Robin comparison for $\beta>0$, or Dirichlet comparison for $\beta=0$, followed by the strong maximum principle gives $D_\beta(t,x)>0$ for $t>0$ and $x>0$. If $\beta>0$ and $D_\beta(t,0)=0$ at a positive time, the boundary Hopf lemma would give $(D_\beta)_x(t,0)>0$, contradicting \eqref{eq:fold-bc}. Thus $D_\beta(t,0)>0$, and the interface law yields \eqref{eq:reflection}. When $\beta=0$, the Hopf lemma instead gives
$j_0(t)=(D_0)_x(t,0)>0$.

For the receiving-side monotonicity, set $v=q_{\beta,x}$. At positive times,
\[
 v_t=v_{xx}+f'(q_\beta)v,\qquad x>0,
 \qquad v(t,0)=-j_\beta(t)<0.
\]
The zero initial condition for this derivative is justified directly from the kernel, even though $u_0$ is only measurable. Indeed, differentiation of \eqref{eq:barrier-kernel} gives
$\sup_{x>0}\int_\mathbb R|\partial_xP_\beta(t,x,y)|\,dy\le Ct^{-1/2}$.
Since $u_0$ vanishes for $y\ge b$ with $b<0$, the initial term and the bounded reaction term in \eqref{eq:mild} therefore give
\[
 \|q_{\beta,x}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty(0,\infty)}
 \le Ct^{-1/2}e^{-c/t}+C\sqrt t\longrightarrow0
 \qquad(t\downarrow0),
\]
where $c>0$. With $M=\|f'\|_{L^\infty([0,1])}$ and $v^+=\max\{v,0\}$, comparison on $[\varepsilon,T]\times(0,\infty)$ gives
\[
 v(t,x)\le e^{M(t-\varepsilon)}
 \|v(\varepsilon,\cdot)^+\|_{L^\infty(0,\infty)},
 \qquad \varepsilon\le t\le T.
\]
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ yields $v\le0$. The strong maximum principle and the strictly negative boundary values give $v<0$ in the interior. Neither concavity of $f$ nor monotonicity of $u_0$ is used.

label: lem:linear-front
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:linear-front}
Fix $0<\rho<1/2$, and set
\[
 a_0=\frac12-\rho,
 \qquad d(\sigma)=e^{-a_0\sigma},
 \qquad \theta_0(\sigma)=\rho d(\sigma)+\frac32e^{-\sigma/2}.
\]
Let $\sigma_0\ge0$, and consider solutions for $\sigma\ge\sigma_0$, $y\ge0$, continuous up to the initial and lateral boundaries and classical in the interior. The initial and boundary values are compatible at $(\sigma_0,0)$, and the solutions are bounded in the respective weighted spaces on every finite time interval.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Suppose that $Q$ solves
\[
 Q_\sigma+\mathcal LQ+\theta_0Q_y=0,\qquad
 Q(\sigma,0)=h(\sigma),
\]
with $Q(\sigma_0,\cdot)\in X_{1/5}$, $h\in C^1([\sigma_0,\infty))$, and
$|h|+|h'|\le M\exp(-c e^{\rho\sigma})$ for fixed $M,c>0$.
If $\sigma_0$ is sufficiently large in terms of $\rho$, then
\begin{equation}\label{front:linear-upper}
 \sup_{\sigma\ge\sigma_0}\|Q(\sigma)\|_{1/5}\le C,
 \qquad
 \sup_{\sigma\ge\sigma_0+1}\sup_{0\le y\le1}|Q_y(\sigma,y)|\le C.
\end{equation}
If the initial and boundary data of $Q$ are nonnegative, then $Q\ge0$, and
$Q(\sigma,2d(\sigma))\le Cd(\sigma)$ for $\sigma\ge\sigma_0+1$.

\item Suppose that $P$, which may change sign, satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{front:linear-positive-cut}
 P_\sigma+\mathcal LP+\vartheta(\sigma)P_y+A(\sigma,y)P=0,
 \qquad P(\sigma,0)=b(\sigma),
\end{equation}
where $\vartheta$, $A$, and $b$ are continuous and, for fixed $M,c>0$,
\[
 |\vartheta(\sigma)|\le Md(\sigma),\quad
 |b(\sigma)|\le Md(\sigma),\quad
 \|A(\sigma,\cdot)\|_\infty
       \le M e^{M\sigma-c e^{\rho\sigma}},\quad
 \sup_{\sigma\ge\sigma_0}\|P(\sigma)\|_{1/6}\le M.
\]
Then there is a real number $\alpha$ such that
\begin{align}
 J(\sigma)&:=\int_0^\infty yP(\sigma,y)\,dy
       \longrightarrow2\sqrt\pi\alpha,
       & |J(\sigma)-2\sqrt\pi\alpha|&\le Cd(\sigma),
       \label{front:linear-moment}\\
 \|P(\sigma)-\alpha\phi\|_{1/6}&\le Cd(\sigma).
       \label{front:linear-profile}
\end{align}
\end{enumerate}
In part~(i), $C$ depends only on $\rho$, $M$, $c$, and an upper bound for $\|Q(\sigma_0)\|_{1/5}$. In part~(ii), it depends only on $\rho$, $\sigma_0$, $M$, and $c$; no derivative bound for $b$ enters the estimates. Thus families with a fixed starting time and common bounds have common constants.

label: front:drift-absorption
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a fixed smooth, compactly supported function $\chi$ with $\chi(0)=1$,
and lift the boundary data in the first part by $h(\sigma)\chi(y)$.
The function $V=Q-h\chi$ has homogeneous boundary data and satisfies
\[
 V_\sigma+\mathcal LV+\theta_0V_y=F,
 \qquad
 \|F(\sigma)\|_{1/5}\le C e^{-c'e^{\rho\sigma}}.
\]
The drift convolution is controlled by
\begin{equation}\label{front:drift-absorption}
 \sup_{\sigma\ge\sigma_0}\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma}
 \bigl[1+(\sigma-s)^{-1/2}\bigr]d(s)\,ds
 \le C_\rho d(\sigma_0).
\end{equation}
Indeed, on $\sigma-s\ge1$ use the integrable tail of $d$, and on $0<\sigma-s<1$ use $d(s)\le d(\sigma_0)$ and the integrability of $(\sigma-s)^{-1/2}$. Since $|\theta_0|\le C_\rho d$, \eqref{front:kernel-bounded}--\eqref{front:kernel-derivative} give, for every finite final time $S$,
\[
 \sup_{\sigma_0\le\sigma\le S}\|V(\sigma)\|_{1/5}
 \le C\|V(\sigma_0)\|_{1/5}
 +C\int_{\sigma_0}^S\|F(s)\|_{1/5}\,ds
 +C e^{-a_0\sigma_0}
       \sup_{\sigma_0\le\sigma\le S}\|V(\sigma)\|_{1/5}.
\]
Taking $\sigma_0$ sufficiently large in terms of $\rho$, we absorb the last term and obtain the Gaussian bound. On $0\le y\le2$, the drift and the lifted forcing are uniformly
bounded. Local parabolic gradient estimates up to the flat boundary, applied to $V$ with homogeneous Dirichlet data on unit time intervals, give the second estimate in \eqref{front:linear-upper}; see~\cite{Lieberman1996} for the standard boundary regularity theory. The bound on $h'$ controls the lifted forcing, and adding back $h\chi$ preserves the gradient estimate.
Consequently, $Q(\sigma,2d)\le h+C(2d)\le Cd$.

The first moment in the second part satisfies the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{front:moment-identity}
 J'=b+\vartheta\int_0^\infty P\,dy
       -\int_0^\infty yAP\,dy.
\end{equation}
The identity can also be obtained from the mild formula using the kernel moment identities above and integration by parts for the drift term. The Gaussian bound justifies the resulting integrals. Thus $|J'|\le Cd$, and integration of the integrable tail gives
\eqref{front:linear-moment}. To prove the profile estimate, separate the
projection \eqref{front:projection} in Duhamel's formula.
The stable part of the initial term is controlled by \eqref{front:kernel-gap}.
For the drift term, use \eqref{front:kernel-derivative} and \eqref{front:kernel-derivative-gap}, interpreting the derivative in the distributional sense.
For the potential term, use
\eqref{front:kernel-bounded}--\eqref{front:kernel-gap}.
Split the boundary term into the most recent unit interval and the preceding
times, and apply the two estimates in \eqref{front:poisson-estimates}.
For $\sigma\ge\sigma_0+1$, the stable terms are bounded in sum by
\[
 C e^{-(\sigma-\sigma_0)}
 +C\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma}
 e^{-(\sigma-s)}d(s)\,ds
 +C\int_{\sigma-1}^{\sigma}
 [1+(\sigma-s)^{-1/2}]d(s)\,ds
 \le Cd(\sigma).
\]
Here we use $a_0<1$; the first unit interval is controlled by the assumed weighted bound on $P$, with a constant depending on $\sigma_0$. Hence
$\|P-\Pi P\|_{1/6}\le Cd$, and the first-moment estimate yields
\eqref{front:linear-profile}.

label: front:positive-cutoff-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\rho$, and write $d(\sigma)=e^{-(1/2-\rho)\sigma}$. By \eqref{eq:uniform-gaussian}, at any fixed positive time the weighted right tail has a Gaussian bound uniform in $\beta$. Choose a common starting time $\sigma_*$ sufficiently large for Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-front} and for the negative cutoff $z=-t^\rho$ to lie in $x>0$ for all subsequent times. Write $t_*=e^{\sigma_*}$. This cutoff uses the bound $u^\beta\le1$ to make the boundary input small:
\[
 0\le w_\beta(\sigma,-d(\sigma))
       \le h(\sigma):=e^{-\sigma/2-e^{\rho\sigma}}.
\]
Remove the nonnegative absorption term from \eqref{front:selfsimilar-equation} and construct a common linear supersolution with boundary value $h$. Its initial profile can be chosen continuous, nonnegative, dominating every $w_\beta(\sigma_*,\cdot)$ on the truncated region, with a common $X_{1/5}$ bound after shifting the boundary to zero, and with value $h(\sigma_*)$ at that boundary. Indeed, take the minimum of the bound $t_*^{-1/2}e^{\sqrt{t_*}\eta}$ and a Gaussian upper envelope furnished by \eqref{eq:uniform-gaussian}, enlarged to be at least $h(\sigma_*)$ at the cutoff. This also ensures initial-boundary compatibility.
Move the negative cutoff to zero by setting $y=\eta+d(\sigma)$.
The drift coefficient is exactly
$\theta_0=\rho d+\frac32e^{-\sigma/2}$, so the first part of
Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-front} applies; $h$ and $h'$ satisfy its required decay bound.
For $\sigma\ge\sigma_*+1$, the gradient bound for the linear supersolution and comparison yield
\begin{equation}\label{front:positive-cutoff-bound}
 w_\beta(\sigma,d(\sigma))\le Cd(\sigma).
\end{equation}
The point $\eta=d$ corresponds to $y=2d$ in the supersolution coordinates. We increase the threshold time $T$ to include this one-unit waiting interval.

The positive cutoff makes the nonlinear potential uniformly small. Move this cutoff to zero and set
\[
 \mathcal P_\beta(\sigma,y)=w_\beta(\sigma,y+d(\sigma)).
\]
The coefficients in \eqref{front:linear-positive-cut} are now
\begin{equation}\label{front:positive-coefficients}
 \vartheta=-\rho d+\frac32e^{-\sigma/2},\qquad
 A_\beta(\sigma,y)=t\frac{g(u^\beta(t,x))}{u^\beta(t,x)}\ge0,
 \qquad x=m(t)+\sqrt t\,(y+d).
\end{equation}
The Gaussian bound for the common supersolution and \eqref{eq:g} give,
on $z\ge t^\rho$,
\[
 0\le A_\beta\le Ctu^\beta
       \le Ct^{3/2}e^{-t^\rho}.
\]
After the shift, the Gaussian bound remains uniform with the weaker weight
$1/6$. Together with \eqref{front:positive-cutoff-bound}, the second part of
Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-front}, started at $\sigma_*+1$, yields a nonnegative amplitude and the profile and first-moment estimates. Positive-time regularity gives continuous coefficients, boundary traces, and compatible initial values at this starting time. The common weighted bound also yields a uniform upper bound for the amplitudes. Returning from $y=\eta-d$ to $\eta$ and weakening the Gaussian
weight slightly once more gives \eqref{front:nonlinear-profile}.
The change of variables also gives the exact identity
\[
 \int_0^\infty y\mathcal P_\beta(\log t,y)\,dy=\mathcal J_\beta(t),
\]
so \eqref{front:uniform-moment} holds with the same common constant. If two different cutoff exponents are used, the resulting profile limits at any fixed $\eta>0$ must agree. Since $\phi(\eta)>0$, their amplitudes coincide; we denote this common value by $\alpha_\beta$.

We now prove strict positivity for each fixed $\beta$. First fix a nonzero function $\psi\in C_c^\infty((1,2))$ with $\psi\ge0$. Choose a time $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_*+1$ sufficiently large that the decaying drift and potential can be absorbed in the homogeneous-boundary Duhamel estimate below and that
\[
 C\|\psi\|_{1/6}\int_{\sigma_1}^\infty
 (|\vartheta|+\|A_\beta\|_\infty)\,d\sigma
 <\frac12\int_0^\infty y\psi(y)\,dy,
\]
where $C$ is the constant in that estimate, independent of sufficiently large $\sigma_1$. Finally, positivity of the transmission kernel and comparison with the linear heat evolution give $\mathcal P_\beta(\sigma_1,y)>0$ for $y>0$. Hence one can choose $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\varepsilon\psi\le \mathcal P_\beta(\sigma_1,\cdot)$.

Let $H$ solve \eqref{front:linear-positive-cut} with the actual coefficients $\vartheta,A_\beta$, homogeneous Dirichlet boundary data, and initial datum $\varepsilon\psi$ at $\sigma_1$. Comparison gives $0\le H\le \mathcal P_\beta$. In Duhamel's formula, \eqref{front:drift-absorption} bounds the drift contribution by $Cd(\sigma_1)$ times the weighted supremum norm. The potential contribution is bounded by $C\int_{\sigma_1}^\infty\|A_\beta(s)\|_\infty\,ds$ times that norm, using \eqref{front:kernel-bounded}. Both coefficients are small for sufficiently large $\sigma_1$. Absorbing these terms gives
\[
 \sup_{\sigma\ge\sigma_1}\|H(\sigma)\|_{1/6}
       \le C\varepsilon\|\psi\|_{1/6}.
\]
By \eqref{front:moment-identity} with zero boundary data, the total variation of its first moment on $[\sigma_1,\infty)$ is at most
\[
 C\varepsilon\|\psi\|_{1/6}
 \int_{\sigma_1}^\infty
 (|\vartheta|+\|A_\beta\|_\infty)\,d\sigma
 <\frac\varepsilon2\int_0^\infty y\psi(y)\,dy.
\]
Thus the limiting first moment of $H$ is positive. Since $H\le \mathcal P_\beta$, this implies $\alpha_\beta>0$. The seed size $\varepsilon$ may depend on $\beta$, so this argument does not assert a positive lower bound uniform over all parameters.

For the intermediate-scale limits, given $\gamma$, choose $0<\rho<\gamma$.
At $\eta=t^{\gamma-1/2}$, the profile error divided by $\eta$ is
$O(t^{\rho-\gamma})$, which proves the first limit in
\eqref{front:intermediate}. For the gradient limit, use the unshifted self-similar coordinates and set
\[
 E_\beta=w_\beta-\alpha_\beta\phi,\qquad
 a(\sigma)=\frac32e^{-\sigma/2},\qquad
 \widetilde A_\beta(\sigma,\eta)
 =t\frac{g(u^\beta(t,m(t)+\sqrt t\eta))}
          {u^\beta(t,m(t)+\sqrt t\eta)}.
\]
Then
\[
 (E_\beta)_\sigma+\mathcal LE_\beta
 +a(E_\beta)_\eta+\widetilde A_\beta E_\beta
 =-\alpha_\beta\bigl(a\phi'+\widetilde A_\beta\phi\bigr).
\]
For $2d(\sigma)\le\eta\le1$ and sufficiently large $\sigma$, take a backward parabolic cylinder with spatial radius $\eta/4$ and time length $(\eta/4)^2$. It remains to the right of the moving positive cutoff, and $d$ is comparable to $d(\sigma)$ throughout it. On this cylinder, \eqref{front:nonlinear-profile} bounds $E_\beta$ by $Cd$, while the potential is superexponentially small and the amplitudes are uniformly bounded. The scaled interior parabolic gradient estimate (see~\cite{Lieberman1996}) therefore gives
\[
 |\partial_\eta E_\beta(\sigma,\eta)|
 \le C\left(\frac d\eta
       +\eta\bigl(e^{-\sigma/2}
          +\|\widetilde A_\beta\|_{L^\infty(\text{cylinder})}\bigr)\right)
 \le C\frac d\eta.
\]
At the intermediate scale above, this yields
$\partial_zv_\beta=\alpha_\beta+o(1)$.
Using $u_x^\beta=e^{-z}(\partial_zv_\beta-v_\beta)$ and dividing by
$z=t^\gamma$ proves the second limit in \eqref{front:intermediate}.

label: cor:signed-amplitudes
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:signed-amplitudes}
Under Assumptions~\ref{hyp:f}--\ref{hyp:data}, fix $0<\rho<1/3$, and set
\[
 \ell(t)=m(t)+t^\rho,\qquad d(\sigma)=e^{-(1/2-\rho)\sigma}.
\]
Choose a common $T_0>1$ sufficiently large that $m(t)-t^\rho>0$ for $t\ge T_0$. Consider a family of classical solutions $W$ on $t>T_0$, $x>0$, continuous up to $t=T_0$ and bounded on each finite time strip, satisfying
\[
 W_t=W_{xx}+c(t,x)W,
\]
where $c$ is continuous, locally bounded, and $c\le1$. In the negative-cutoff coordinates, define
\[
 Z_W(\sigma,y)=t^{-1/2}e^{\sqrt t\,(y-d(\sigma))}
 W\!\left(t,m(t)+\sqrt t\,(y-d(\sigma))\right),
 \qquad t=e^\sigma,\quad y\ge0.
\]
Suppose that common constants $M,c_0>0$ give
\[
 |Z_W(\sigma,0)|\le M e^{-c_0e^{\rho\sigma}}
 \quad(\sigma\ge\log T_0),\qquad
 \|Z_W(\log T_0,\cdot)\|_{1/5}\le M.
\]
For each member of the family, suppose also that there are finite $\beta_1,\beta_2\ge0$ such that
\[
 |1-c(t,x)|\le M\bigl(u^{\beta_1}(t,x)+u^{\beta_2}(t,x)\bigr),
 \qquad t\ge T_0,\quad x\ge\ell(t).
\]
Then each $W$ has a real amplitude $\alpha_W$, and there are common constants $C,T$ such that $|\alpha_W|\le C$ and, for $t\ge T$,
\begin{equation}\label{front:signed-moment}
 \left|e^{-2t}\int_{\ell(t)}^\infty
 (x-\ell(t))e^xW(t,x)\,dx-2\sqrt\pi\alpha_W\right|
 \le Ct^{\rho-1/2}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, defining
\[
 P_W(\log t,y)=t e^{x-2t}W(t,x),
 \qquad x=\ell(t)+\sqrt t\,y,
\]
we have $\|P_W(\log t,\cdot)-\alpha_W\phi\|_{1/6}\le Ct^{\rho-1/2}$. For each $\rho<\gamma<1/3$,
\begin{equation}\label{front:signed-intermediate}
 \frac{e^{t^\gamma}W(t,m(t)+t^\gamma)}{t^\gamma}
 \longrightarrow\alpha_W,
\end{equation}
uniformly over the family. The constants depend only on $f,u_0,\rho,T_0,M,c_0$, and not on the individual solution or the parameters $\beta_1,\beta_2$.

title: Proof
body_md:
To obtain Kato's inequality, use the smooth convex approximation
$\Phi_\delta(s)=\sqrt{s^2+\delta^2}$. The equation for $W$ gives
\[
 (\partial_t-\partial_{xx})\Phi_\delta(W)
 =cW\Phi_\delta'(W)-\Phi_\delta''(W)|W_x|^2
 \le cW\Phi_\delta'(W).
\]
Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ against nonnegative compactly supported test
functions yields
$\partial_t|W|-\partial_{xx}|W|\le c|W|\le|W|$ in distributions.
The same argument for an additional bounded source $F$ gives the upper
bound $c|W|+|F|$, a form used in Section~\ref{sec:small-beta}.
At the negative cutoff, prescribe the smooth upper envelope
\[
 h(\sigma)=M_1\exp(-c_0e^{\rho\sigma}),\qquad
 |h|+|h'|\le C\exp\bigl(-(c_0/2)e^{\rho\sigma}\bigr).
\]
Choose $M_1$ large enough, in terms of the common data, that $h(\log T_0)\ge M$. Then $h(\log T_0)e^{-y^2/5}$ is a common dominating initial profile in the shifted negative-cutoff coordinates, compatible with $h$ at $y=0$. The linear supersolution construction used in the preceding subsection applies to $|W|$. If necessary, propagate this common supersolution to a later fixed time before applying Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-front}(i). On this finite interval, the kernel estimates and a Volterra Gronwall estimate with the integrable singularity $(\sigma-s)^{-1/2}$ preserve a common $X_{1/5}$ bound. Thus the bound at the later starting time depends only on the listed common data. After a further one-unit waiting interval, its gradient bound over the distance $2d$ between the cutoffs gives
\[
 |P_W(\sigma,0)|\le Cd(\sigma),\qquad
 \|P_W(\sigma,\cdot)\|_{1/6}\le C.
\]
No derivative estimate for the actual boundary trace of $W$ is needed.

In the positive-cutoff coordinates, direct calculation gives
\[
 (P_W)_\sigma+\mathcal LP_W
 +\left(-\rho d+\frac32e^{-\sigma/2}\right)(P_W)_y
 +A_WP_W=0,
 \qquad A_W(\sigma,y)=t(1-c(t,x)).
\]
The coefficient assumption and the preceding nonlinear estimates imply
\[
 0\le A_W\le Mt\bigl(u^{\beta_1}+u^{\beta_2}\bigr)
 \le Ct^{3/2}e^{-t^\rho},\qquad x\ge\ell(t).
\]
Thus all bounds in Lemma~\ref{lem:linear-front}(ii) hold with common constants, and positive-time continuity gives compatible initial and boundary traces at the chosen starting time. That lemma yields the asserted profile estimate and a bounded family of real amplitudes. The identity
\[
 \int_0^\infty yP_W(\log t,y)\,dy
 =e^{-2t}\int_{\ell(t)}^\infty(x-\ell(t))e^xW(t,x)\,dx
\]
gives \eqref{front:signed-moment}. Finally, for $\gamma>\rho$, set $y=t^{\gamma-1/2}-d$. The profile error, after division by $t^{\gamma-1/2}$, is $O(t^{\rho-\gamma})$, while $y/t^{\gamma-1/2}\to1$ and $\phi(y)/y\to1$. This proves \eqref{front:signed-intermediate} uniformly.

label: matching:energy-lemma
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: matching:weighted-equation
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $q=q_{\mathrm{aux}}$. Standard parabolic theory, after mapping the moving interval to a fixed interval, gives the bounded solution and positive-time regularity; see~\cite{Lieberman1996}. Comparison gives $0\le q\le1$. All energy calculations below start at $T+1$, so initial corner incompatibilities cause no difficulty. The identities may first be derived for smooth data and then justified by approximation on time intervals separated from $T$.
Recall $g(s)=s-f(s)$ from~\eqref{eq:g}, and set
\[
 G(s)=\int_0^s g(r)\,dr,\qquad V(t,z)=e^zq(t,z).
\]
By \eqref{eq:g}, $0\le g(s)\le Cs^2$, hence $0\le G(s)\le Cs^3$.
The function $V$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{matching:weighted-equation}
 V_t-V_{zz}+a(t)(V_z-V)+P_V(z,V)=0,
 \qquad a(t)=\frac3{2t},
\end{equation}
where
\[
 P(z,V)=e^{2z}G(e^{-z}V),\qquad
 P_V(z,V)=e^zg(e^{-z}V)\ge0.
\]
The right boundary condition becomes $V(t,R(t))=\alpha R(t)$, corresponding to the linear leading-edge growth $V\sim\alpha z$. Its gradient energy on the positive half of the interval has the leading contribution $\alpha^2R(t)/2$. Subtracting this contribution, define
\begin{equation}\label{matching:renormalized-energy}
 E(t)=\int_{-R(t)}^{R(t)}
 \left(\frac12V_z^2+P(z,V)\right)\,dz
 -\frac{\alpha^2}2R(t).
\end{equation}
Using that boundary condition and completing the square gives
\begin{align}\label{matching:coercive-identity}
 E(t)+\alpha
 ={}&\frac12\int_{-R(t)}^0V_z^2\,dz
 +\frac12\int_0^{R(t)}(V_z-\alpha)^2\,dz \notag\\
 &+\int_{-R(t)}^{R(t)}P(z,V)\,dz
 +\alpha[1-V(t,0)].
\end{align}
Since $V(t,0)=q(t,0)\le1$, every term on the right is nonnegative.
In particular, $E\ge-\alpha$.

The energy also controls the norm needed to estimate the drift term.
On the negative half of the interval we use $V\le e^z$; on the positive half we use
\[
 V(t,z)=V(t,0)+\alpha z
 +\int_0^z[V_z(t,s)-\alpha]\,ds.
\]
The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and~\eqref{matching:coercive-identity} give
\begin{equation}\label{matching:drift-control}
 \int_{-R(t)}^{R(t)}(V_z-V)^2\,dz
 \le CR(t)^2[E(t)+\alpha+1]+CR(t)^3.
\end{equation}
The constants below may depend on $\alpha,T,\gamma,f$ and $\|h'\|_{L^\infty([T,\infty))}$, but not on $t$. The resulting energy and dissipation bounds may additionally depend on the initial profile through the finite energy $E(T+1)$.

Differentiate~\eqref{matching:renormalized-energy} and use
\eqref{matching:weighted-equation} to eliminate $V_{zz}-P_V$.
The interior contribution is
\[
 -\int_{-R}^R V_t^2\,dz
 -a(t)\int_{-R}^R(V_z-V)V_t\,dz.
\]
At the moving right endpoint, $V_t+R'V_z=\alpha R'$.
Thus the right boundary contribution, including the renormalization term, is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{matching:right-boundary-flux}
 -\frac{R'}2[V_z(t,R)-\alpha]^2
 +R'P(R,\alpha R).
\end{equation}
Since $P(R,\alpha R)\le C\alpha^3R^3e^{-R}$, its positive part is integrable.
At the left endpoint, write $b(t)=e^{-R(t)}h(t)$. Differentiation along this moving endpoint gives
\[
 V_t(t,-R)-R'V_z(t,-R)=b'(t).
\]
The corresponding boundary contribution is
\begin{equation}\label{matching:left-boundary-flux}
 -V_z(t,-R)b'(t)-\frac{R'}2V_z(t,-R)^2
 +R'P(-R,b).
\end{equation}
Since $R'(t)>0$, Young's inequality gives directly
\[
 -V_z(t,-R)b'-\frac{R'}2V_z(t,-R)^2
 \le\frac{|b'|^2}{2R'}.
\]
Here $b'=e^{-R}(h'-R'h)$ and $P(-R,b)=e^{-2R}G(h)$. Hence the positive part of \eqref{matching:left-boundary-flux} is bounded by
\[
 \frac{|b'|^2}{2R'}+R'P(-R,b)
 \le C\bigl(t^{1-\gamma}+t^{\gamma-1}\bigr)e^{-2t^\gamma},
\]
which is integrable. This polynomial factor can be absorbed into a weaker exponential bound $Ce^{-R(t)}$.

Use Young's inequality to absorb the drift term into the dissipation.
Together with~\eqref{matching:drift-control}, this gives
\begin{align}\label{matching:energy-dissipation}
 E'(t)\le{}&-\frac12\int_{-R(t)}^{R(t)}V_t^2\,dz
 +Ct^{2\gamma-2}[E(t)+\alpha+1] \notag\\
 &+Ct^{3\gamma-2}+C(1+R(t)^3)e^{-R(t)}.
\end{align}
Both $t^{2\gamma-2}$ and $t^{3\gamma-2}$ are integrable, the latter being the term that requires $\gamma<1/3$; the exponential remainder is integrable as well. Apply Gronwall's inequality to $E+\alpha+1\ge1$,
and then integrate~\eqref{matching:energy-dissipation}, to obtain
\begin{equation}\label{matching:finite-dissipation}
 \sup_{t\ge T+1}E(t)<\infty,\qquad
 \int_{T+1}^\infty\int_{-R(t)}^{R(t)}V_t^2\,dz\,dt<\infty.
\end{equation}

We next identify the limits of time translates. Take any sequence $t_n\to\infty$. On fixed compact subsets of space-time, $0\le q\le1$ and interior parabolic estimates give local compactness of $V(t_n+s,z)$. After passing to a subsequence, these functions and their first spatial derivatives converge uniformly on compact subsets. For fixed $K,S>0$, the expanding domain eventually contains $[-K,K]$ throughout $[t_n-S,t_n+S]$, and \eqref{matching:finite-dissipation} yields
\[
 \int_{t_n-S}^{t_n+S}\int_{-K}^K|V_t(t,z)|^2\,dz\,dt
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus every subsequential limit is independent of $s$. Passing to the limit in the equation in the distributional sense, using $a(t_n+s)\to0$ uniformly for bounded $s$, and then applying local regularity, we find that its stationary profile $V_\infty$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{matching:stationary-limit}
 V_\infty''=e^zg(e^{-z}V_\infty),\qquad
 0\le e^{-z}V_\infty\le1.
\end{equation}
By~\eqref{matching:coercive-identity} and the uniform energy bound, we may first pass to the limit on $[0,K]$ and then let $K\to\infty$ to obtain
\begin{equation}\label{matching:tail-slope-control}
 \int_0^\infty[V_\infty'(z)-\alpha]^2\,dz<\infty.
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{matching:stationary-limit} shows that $V_\infty'$ is nondecreasing.
Consequently,~\eqref{matching:tail-slope-control} forces
\begin{equation}\label{matching:identified-slope}
 \lim_{z\to\infty}V_\infty'(z)=\alpha,
 \qquad V_\infty(z)=\alpha z+o(z).
\end{equation}
In particular, $V_\infty\not\equiv0$.

It remains to identify this stationary profile as a translated wave. Set $Q=e^{-z}V_\infty$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{matching:wave-ode}
 Q''+2Q'+f(Q)=0,\qquad 0\le Q\le1,\qquad Q(+\infty)=0.
\end{equation}
To identify the limit at the other end, set $F(s)=\int_0^s f(r)\,dr$.
Local ODE estimates give a uniform bound on the derivative of the bounded
solution $Q$, whose mechanical energy satisfies
\[
 \frac d{dz}\left(\frac12Q'^2+F(Q)\right)=-2Q'^2.
\]
The energy has finite limits at both ends, so $Q'\in L^2(\mathbb R)$.
The boundedness of $Q''=-2Q'-f(Q)$ makes $Q'$ uniformly continuous,
and therefore $Q'(\pm\infty)=0$. The boundedness of
$Q'''=-2Q''-f'(Q)Q'$ also makes $Q''$ uniformly continuous. Together with the finite limits of $Q'$ at both ends, this implies $Q''(\pm\infty)=0$: otherwise, uniform continuity would force changes of a fixed size in $Q'$ along intervals escaping to one of the two ends. The ODE therefore gives $f(Q(z))\to0$. For every $0<\delta<1/2$, positivity of $f$ on $[\delta,1-\delta]$ implies that $Q$ eventually avoids this interval at either end. Continuity prevents repeated transitions between the neighborhoods of $0$ and $1$ on either tail. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ shows that each end limit exists and is either $0$ or $1$. If $Q(-\infty)=0$, both limiting
energies vanish, and the energy identity forces $Q'\equiv0$, contradicting
\eqref{matching:identified-slope}. Thus $Q(-\infty)=1$. The strong maximum
principle gives $0<Q<1$. At any point where $Q'=0$, one has
$Q''=-f(Q)<0$, so every critical point would be a strict local maximum. If $Q'$ were positive somewhere, it would remain positive to the left, since a transition from negative to positive would require a local minimum. This contradicts $Q(-\infty)=1$ and $Q<1$. Thus $Q'\le0$, and a zero of $Q'$ would itself force positive values immediately to its left. Hence $Q'<0$.
By the classical uniqueness recalled with~\eqref{eq:wave}, $Q(z)=U_*(z-\xi)$.

The expansion of the wave tail gives
\[
 \lim_{z\to\infty}\frac{e^zU_*(z-\xi)}z=A_*e^\xi.
\]
Comparison with~\eqref{matching:identified-slope} yields
$\xi=\log(\alpha/A_*)$. Every subsequence of time translates has the
same stationary limit. Hence the full family converges locally uniformly,
as asserted in~\eqref{matching:auxiliary-limit}.

body_md:
Fix a finite $\beta\ge0$, choose $0<\gamma<1/3$, and set $R(t)=t^\gamma$. Given $0<\varepsilon<\alpha_\beta$, Lemma~\ref{lem:leading-edge} allows us to choose $T$ sufficiently large that
\begin{equation}\label{phase:front-amplitude-bracket}
 (\alpha_\beta-\varepsilon)R(t)e^{-R(t)}
 \le u^\beta(t,m(t)+R(t))
 \le(\alpha_\beta+\varepsilon)R(t)e^{-R(t)},
 \qquad t\ge T.
\end{equation}
Increase $T$ if necessary so that the moving interval stays a fixed positive distance from the interface and $(\alpha_\beta+\varepsilon)R(t)e^{-R(t)}\le1$ for all $t\ge T$.

Set $\widehat u_\beta(t,z)=u^\beta(t,m(t)+z)$. Since $m'(t)=2-3/(2t)$, this function satisfies the same equation as the auxiliary solutions in \eqref{matching:auxiliary-equation}. We apply Lemma~\ref{matching:energy-lemma} with amplitudes $\alpha_\beta\pm\varepsilon$, common initial data
\[
 q_{\mathrm{aux}}^\pm(T,z)=\widehat u_\beta(T,z),\qquad |z|<R(T),
\]
and common left boundary data
\[
 h(t)=u^\beta(t,m(t)-R(t)).
\]
These data lie in $[0,1]$. Moreover,
\[
 h'(t)=u_t^\beta(t,m(t)-R(t))
 +(m'(t)-R'(t))u_x^\beta(t,m(t)-R(t)).
\]
Interior parabolic estimates away from the interface bound $u_t^\beta$ and $u_x^\beta$ along this curve, while $m'-R'$ is bounded. Thus $h\in C^1([T,\infty))$ has bounded derivative, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed $\beta$. All hypotheses of the matching lemma are satisfied. Possible incompatibilities at the initial right corners are covered by its formulation.

The two auxiliary problems have the same initial profile and left boundary value as $\widehat u_\beta$, and their right boundary values bracket its trace by \eqref{phase:front-amplitude-bracket}. Comparison therefore gives
\[
 q_{\mathrm{aux}}^-(t,z)
 \le\widehat u_\beta(t,z)
 \le q_{\mathrm{aux}}^+(t,z),\qquad t>T,\quad |z|\le R(t).
\]
For every fixed $K>0$, the matching lemma gives uniform convergence of these two bounds on $[-K,K]$ to
\[
 U_*\!\left(z-\log\frac{\alpha_\beta-\varepsilon}{A_*}\right)
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 U_*\!\left(z-\log\frac{\alpha_\beta+\varepsilon}{A_*}\right),
\]
respectively. Both profiles tend uniformly on $[-K,K]$ to $U_*(z-\xi_\beta)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Taking $t\to\infty$ first and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in the comparison yields
\begin{equation}\label{phase:local-wave-limit}
 u^\beta(t,m(t)+z)\longrightarrow U_*(z-\xi_\beta),
 \qquad \xi_\beta=\log\frac{\alpha_\beta}{A_*},
\end{equation}
locally uniformly in $z$.

We extend this convergence to the entire receiving half-line using \eqref{eq:right-monotone}. Fix $K>0$ and take $t$ large enough that $m(t)>K$. On $0\le x\le m(t)-K$, their deviations from $1$ are controlled by the values at $x=m(t)-K$, since
\[
 u^\beta(t,m(t)-K)\le u^\beta(t,x)\le1,
 \qquad U_*(-K-\xi_\beta)\le U_*(x-m(t)-\xi_\beta)\le1.
\]
At $x=0$, these inequalities are understood using the right-hand trace. On $x\ge m(t)+K$, their values are controlled by those at $x=m(t)+K$, since
\[
 0\le u^\beta(t,x)\le u^\beta(t,m(t)+K),
 \qquad 0\le U_*(x-m(t)-\xi_\beta)\le U_*(K-\xi_\beta).
\]
On the intervening interval, \eqref{phase:local-wave-limit} gives uniform convergence. Consequently,
\[
 \limsup_{t\to\infty}\sup_{x\ge0}
 |u^\beta(t,x)-U_*(x-m(t)-\xi_\beta)|
 \le\max\{1-U_*(-K-\xi_\beta),\,U_*(K-\xi_\beta)\}.
\]
Letting $K\to\infty$ proves \eqref{phase:uniform-wave}.

Finally, suppose that another phase $\widetilde\xi_\beta$ gives the same convergence. Evaluating both limits at $x=m(t)+z$ for any fixed $z$ yields
\[
 U_*(z-\xi_\beta)=U_*(z-\widetilde\xi_\beta).
\]
Strict monotonicity of $U_*$ implies $\widetilde\xi_\beta=\xi_\beta$, proving uniqueness.

body_md:
Fix $\beta\in[0,\infty)$ and $\eta\in(0,1)$, and set $z_\eta=U_*^{-1}(\eta)$.
For every fixed $R>0$,~\eqref{phase:uniform-wave} and $m(t)\to\infty$ imply
$u^\beta(t,R)\to1$. Thus the set in~\eqref{eq:arrival} is nonempty, and
$T_\eta^\beta(R)<\infty$ for every $R>0$.

The same convergence gives $u^\beta(t,0^+)\to1$, whereas
\eqref{phase:finite-time-tail} implies $u^\beta(t,x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$
for each fixed $t>0$. Continuity and strict spatial monotonicity therefore
provide a unique positive level-set position $X_\eta^\beta(t)$ for all
sufficiently large $t$. To locate it, fix $\delta>0$. Since
\[
 U_*(z_\eta-\delta)>\eta>U_*(z_\eta+\delta),
\]
\eqref{phase:uniform-wave} gives, for all sufficiently large $t$,
\[
 u^\beta(t,m(t)+\xi_\beta+z_\eta-\delta)>\eta,
 \qquad
 u^\beta(t,m(t)+\xi_\beta+z_\eta+\delta)<\eta.
\]
Both spatial arguments are then positive. Strict spatial monotonicity places
$X_\eta^\beta(t)$ between them. As $\delta>0$ is arbitrary, this proves
\begin{equation}\label{phase:level-location}
 \begin{gathered}
 u^\beta(t,X_\eta^\beta(t))=\eta,\\
 X_\eta^\beta(t)=m(t)+\xi_\beta+z_\eta+o(1).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}

For a fixed $\delta>0$, choose $T_\delta$ large enough that $m$ is strictly
increasing on $[T_\delta,\infty)$ and
\[
 |X_\eta^\beta(t)-m(t)-\xi_\beta-z_\eta|<\delta,
 \qquad t\ge T_\delta.
\]
For sufficiently large $R$,~\eqref{phase:finite-time-tail} gives
$u^\beta(t,R)<\eta$ for $0<t\le T_\delta$. Since $m(t)\to\infty$, the equations
\[
 m(t_-(R))+\xi_\beta+z_\eta=R-\delta,
 \qquad
 m(t_+(R))+\xi_\beta+z_\eta=R+\delta
\]
have unique roots in $[T_\delta,\infty)$, with
$T_\delta<t_-(R)<t_+(R)$, once $R$ is sufficiently large.
For $T_\delta\le t\le t_-(R)$, we have
\[
 X_\eta^\beta(t)<m(t)+\xi_\beta+z_\eta+\delta\le R,
\]
hence $u^\beta(t,R)<\eta$. At $t=t_+(R)$, we instead have
$X_\eta^\beta(t)>m(t)+\xi_\beta+z_\eta-\delta=R$, hence
$u^\beta(t,R)>\eta$. Together with the exclusion of arrivals before
$T_\delta$, these inequalities yield
\begin{equation}\label{phase:arrival-bracket}
 t_-(R)\le T_\eta^\beta(R)\le t_+(R).
\end{equation}
Applying the increasing function $m$ to this bracket gives
\[
 R-\xi_\beta-z_\eta-\delta
 \le m(T_\eta^\beta(R))
 \le R-\xi_\beta-z_\eta+\delta.
\]
Since this holds for every $\delta>0$ and all sufficiently large $R$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{phase:arrival-inverse}
 m(T_\eta^\beta(R))=R-\xi_\beta-z_\eta+o(1).
\end{equation}

Apply the same argument with $\beta=0$ and subtract the two identities.
The mean value theorem gives a point $\theta_R$ between the two arrival
times such that
\[
 m'(\theta_R)\big(T_\eta^\beta(R)-T_\eta^0(R)\big)
 =\xi_0-\xi_\beta+o(1).
\]
If the arrival times coincide, take $\theta_R$ equal to their common value.
By~\eqref{phase:finite-time-tail}, both arrival times tend to infinity as
$R\to\infty$. Hence $\theta_R\to\infty$ and
$m'(\theta_R)=2-3/(2\theta_R)\to2$, proving~\eqref{phase:delay-formula}.
The level-dependent term $z_\eta$ cancels upon subtraction, so the limiting
delay is independent of $\eta$.

label: small:kernel-variation
title: Proof
body_md:
Use the transmission kernel~\eqref{eq:barrier-kernel}, with $P_0(t)=G_t$.
We use the same notation for these kernels and their integral operators.
Differentiating its integral representation from the right at $\beta=0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{small:kernel-variation}
 \mathcal B_t(x,y)=-\frac{\operatorname{sgn}(x)\operatorname{sgn}(y)}2G'_t(|x|+|y|).
\end{equation}
At the interface, signs are interpreted through one-sided limits. Write
$\mathcal D_\beta(t)=(P_\beta(t)-G_t)/\beta$ for $\beta>0$.
The mean-value formula and integration of $|G'_t|$ give
\begin{equation}\label{small:kernel-quotient}
 \|\mathcal D_\beta(t)\|_{L^\infty\to L^\infty},\quad
 \|\mathcal B_t\|_{L^\infty\to L^\infty}
 \le\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi t}}.
\end{equation}
Subtracting $G'_t(|x|+|y|)$ from its translated value in the mean-value formula also gives
\[
 \|\mathcal D_\beta(t)-\mathcal B_t\|_{L^\infty\to L^\infty}
 \le C\beta\|G''_t\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}\le C\beta/t.
\]
In particular, convergence holds in operator norm uniformly on $[\delta,T]$ for every $0<\delta<T$.

The initial term admits a stronger bound near $t=0$. With $d=-b>0$ from
Assumption~\ref{hyp:data}, $u_0$ is supported in $(-\infty,-d]$.
Integrating $|G'_t|$ over this region yields
\begin{equation}\label{small:initial-kernel-bound}
 \|\mathcal D_\beta(t)u_0\|_\infty+\|\mathcal B_tu_0\|_\infty
 \le Ct^{-1/2}e^{-d^2/(4t)},\qquad \beta>0.
\end{equation}
Splitting $[0,T]$ at a small positive time and then using operator-norm
convergence away from zero shows that
\[
 \sup_{0<t\le T}\|(\mathcal D_\beta(t)-\mathcal B_t)u_0\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.
\]
For the reaction term, split the time integral according to whether
$t-s<\delta$ or $t-s\ge\delta$. The first part is bounded by $C\sqrt\delta$
uniformly for $t\le T$, by~\eqref{small:kernel-quotient}; the second tends to
zero by operator-norm convergence. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{small:forcing-convergence}
 \sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\|
 \int_0^t(\mathcal D_\beta(t-s)-\mathcal B_{t-s})f(U(s))\,ds
 \right\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}

Fix $\beta_*>0$ and put $W_\beta=(u^\beta-U)/\beta$, with $W_\beta(0)=0$.
Subtracting the two nonlinear Duhamel formulas gives
\[
 W_\beta(t)=\mathcal D_\beta(t)u_0
 +\int_0^t\mathcal D_\beta(t-s)f(U(s))\,ds
 +\int_0^t P_\beta(t-s)\frac{f(u^\beta(s))-f(U(s))}{\beta}\,ds.
\]
The contraction bound for $P_\beta$, the Lipschitz continuity of $f$, and
\eqref{small:initial-kernel-bound} imply, by Gronwall's inequality,
\begin{equation}\label{small:finite-quotient-bound}
 \sup_{0<\beta\le\beta_*}\sup_{0\le t\le T}
 \|W_\beta(t)\|_\infty\le C_T.
\end{equation}
Here and below the constants may depend on $f,u_0,T$, but not on
$\beta\in(0,\beta_*]$.
Define $w$ as the unique bounded solution, on each finite time interval, of
\begin{equation}\label{small:variation-duhamel}
 \begin{split}
 w(t)={}&\mathcal B_tu_0+\int_0^t\mathcal B_{t-s}f(U(s))\,ds\\
 &+\int_0^tG_{t-s}\bigl[f'(U(s))w(s)\bigr]\,ds.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Existence and uniqueness follow by successive approximation for this linear
Volterra equation; uniqueness makes these solutions consistent as $T$ varies.
The first two terms tend to zero in $L^\infty$ as $t\downarrow0$, by
\eqref{small:initial-kernel-bound} and~\eqref{small:kernel-quotient}, so
$\|w(t)\|_\infty\to0$ as well.

Taylor's formula gives
\[
 \left\|\frac{f(u^\beta)-f(U)}\beta-f'(U)W_\beta\right\|_\infty
 \le\frac12\|f''\|_\infty\beta\|W_\beta\|_\infty^2.
\]
When the integral equations for $W_\beta$ and $w$ are subtracted, the
initial and reaction forcing errors tend to zero uniformly on $[0,T]$
by the estimates above. The additional semigroup error is bounded by
\[
 \left\|\int_0^t(P_\beta(t-s)-G_{t-s})[f'(U(s))w(s)]\,ds\right\|_\infty
 \le C_T\beta\sqrt T.
\]
The Taylor remainder contributes at most $C_T\beta T$, and the remaining
term is bounded by $\|f'\|_\infty\int_0^t\|W_\beta(s)-w(s)\|_\infty\,ds$.
Another application of Gronwall's inequality proves uniform convergence
$W_\beta\to w$ on $[0,T]$, establishing~\eqref{small:finite-expansion}.

We next record a spatial bound needed for the later amplitude analysis.
The same kernel representation gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\mathcal D_\beta(t,x,y)|\,dy\le G_t(x),
 \qquad 0\le P_\beta(t,x,y)\le2G_t(x-y).
\]
With $M=\|f'\|_\infty$, the difference-quotient equation therefore yields
\[
 |W_\beta(t,x)|\le CG_t(x)+C\int_0^tG_r(x)\,dr
 +2M\int_0^t(G_{t-s}*|W_\beta(s)|)(x)\,ds.
\]
Iterating this inequality and using the Gaussian convolution identity gives
\[
 |W_\beta(T,x)|\le Ce^{2MT}G_T(x)
 +C\int_0^T e^{2Mr}G_r(x)\,dr.
\]
Since $e^{-x^2/(4r)}\le e^{-x^2/(4T)}$ for $r\le T$ and
$\int_0^T r^{-1/2}\,dr=2\sqrt T$, we conclude that
\begin{equation}\label{small:finite-gaussian}
 |W_\beta(T,x)|\le C_Te^{-x^2/(4T)},
 \qquad 0<\beta\le\beta_*,\quad x\ne0.
\end{equation}
The same bound holds for $w(T,x)$ by passage to the limit.
For any fixed, sufficiently large starting time $T_0$ and fixed cutoff
exponent $\rho$, the negative-cutoff normalization $Z_{W_\beta}$ in
Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-amplitudes} consequently satisfies
$\sup_{0<\beta\le\beta_*}\|Z_{W_\beta}(\log T_0,\cdot)\|_{1/5}<\infty$.
Indeed, after that change of variables the bound is a Gaussian with quadratic
exponent $-y^2/4$ and a linear term, which is absorbed by the weaker weight
$e^{y^2/5}$. This is an initial weighted bound at the fixed time $T_0$.

It remains to identify the equation and interface traces of $w$.
For a bounded Lipschitz function $\phi$, direct integration of
\eqref{small:kernel-variation} gives, for $r>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{small:kernel-traces}
 [\mathcal B_r\phi]=\partial_x(G_r*\phi)(0),\qquad
 [\partial_x\mathcal B_r\phi]=0.
\end{equation}
These trace identities also hold for bounded measurable $\phi$ when $r>0$
is fixed. To justify taking traces under the time integral in
\eqref{small:variation-duhamel}, fix $t>0$ and split it at $s=t/2$.
For $s\le t/2$, all kernel derivatives involved are integrable with bounds
away from $r=t-s=0$. For $s\ge t/2$, $f(U(s,\cdot))$ has a common spatial
Lipschitz bound. In fact, writing $a=|x|$ gives on either side of the interface
\[
 \partial_x\mathcal B_r\phi(x)
 =-\frac12\int_0^\infty G''_r(a+y)[\phi(y)-\phi(-y)]\,dy,
\]
and thus
\[
 \sup_{x\ne0}|\partial_x\mathcal B_r\phi(x)|
 \le C\operatorname{Lip}(\phi)r^{-1/2}.
\]
This integrable bound permits passage to both derivative traces; the traces
of $\mathcal B_r\phi$ itself are controlled by~\eqref{small:kernel-quotient}.
The last, ordinary heat-potential term in~\eqref{small:variation-duhamel}
has continuous value and first spatial derivative across zero, since its
source is bounded and $\|G'_r\|_1\le Cr^{-1/2}$.
Taking jumps in~\eqref{small:variation-duhamel} and using the Duhamel formula
for $U$ therefore gives
\[
 [w](t)=\partial_x(G_t*u_0)(0)
 +\int_0^t\partial_x(G_{t-s}*f(U(s)))(0)\,ds=U_x(t,0),
 \qquad [w_x](t)=0.
\]
Away from the interface, $\mathcal B_r$ solves the heat equation and its
initial action vanishes locally as $r\downarrow0$. The integral equation
and interior parabolic regularity then give $w_t=w_{xx}+f'(U)w$ on each
half-line for positive times. Equivalently, in distributions,
\begin{equation}\label{small:distributional-variation}
 w_t=w_{xx}+f'(U)w-U_x(t,0)\delta'_0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the distributional second derivative contributes
$[w_x]\delta_0+[w]\delta'_0$ in addition to the piecewise second derivative.
The difference of two solutions in the stated class has zero jumps, solves
the homogeneous full-line equation with bounded potential $f'(U)$, and has
zero initial data. Full-line uniqueness therefore proves the asserted
uniqueness for~\eqref{small:variation-problem}.

body_md:
The parameter order and the reflection comparison give
\[
 q_\beta\ge q_{\beta_*},\qquad p_\beta\ge q_\beta.
\]
Fix $0<c_{\rm in}<c_{\rm out}<2$. Spatial monotonicity gives
\[
 u^\beta(t,x)\ge q_{\beta_*}(t,|x|)
 \ge q_{\beta_*}(t,c_{\rm out}t),\qquad |x|\le c_{\rm out}t,
\]
with one-sided traces at zero. Since $c_{\rm out}<2$, phase convergence for
the fixed parameter $\beta_*$ makes the last expression tend to $1$.
Thus, for every sufficiently small $\delta>0$, there is a common starting
time beyond which
\[
 1-\delta\le u^\beta(t,x)\le1\qquad (|x|\le c_{\rm out}t).
\]
Choose $a_*>0$ so that
\[
 f(s)\ge a_*(1-s),\qquad f'(s)\le-a_*\qquad (1-\delta\le s\le1).
\]
Thus $1-u^\beta$ satisfies $(\partial_t-\partial_{xx}+a_*)(1-u^\beta)\le0$ in this interval. Choose $b_*>0$ such that $b_*^2+b_*c_{\rm out}<a_*$. The even function
\begin{equation}\label{small:saturation-screen}
 \Psi(t,x)=C e^{-a_*(t-T)}+C e^{-b_*c_{\rm out}t}\cosh(b_*x)
\end{equation}
satisfies
\[
 (\partial_t-\partial_{xx}+a_*)\Psi
 =C(a_*-b_*c_{\rm out}-b_*^2)e^{-b_*c_{\rm out}t}\cosh(b_*x)\ge0.
\]
It is continuous at zero with $\Psi_x(t,0)=0$, so it satisfies the interface
conditions for every $\beta$. Choose $T$ above the common starting time.
The first term controls the initial section $t=T$, while
$e^{-b_*c_{\rm out}t}\cosh(b_*c_{\rm out}t)\ge1/2$ at each lateral endpoint.
Thus a common choice of $C$ bounds $1-u^\beta$ on the parabolic boundary.
On $|x|\le c_{\rm in}t$, the spatial term is at most
$Ce^{-b_*(c_{\rm out}-c_{\rm in})t}$. The comparison principle gives
\begin{equation}\label{small:inner-saturation}
 1-u^\beta(t,x)\le Ce^{-\omega t},\qquad |x|\le c_{\rm in}t.
\end{equation}

Let $\mathsf S_\beta(r)$ denote the transmission heat operator, and write
$F_\beta(t)=f(u^\beta(t))$. Differentiating~\eqref{eq:barrier-kernel}
in the heat time, each Gaussian term is controlled after spatial integration
by $\|\partial_rG_r\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}\le C/r$.
The translated Gaussian terms have the same bound, and their averaging
weight has total mass $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}\,ds=1$.
Consequently, for $r,h>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{small:heat-time-bounds}
 \|\partial_r\mathsf S_\beta(r)\|_{\infty\to\infty}\le \frac Cr,
 \qquad
 \|\mathsf S_\beta(r+h)-\mathsf S_\beta(r)\|_{\infty\to\infty}
 \le C\min\{1,h/r\},
\end{equation}
uniformly in $\beta$. For the second estimate, integrate the first when
$h\le r$, and otherwise use the contraction bound. Apply Duhamel's formula
on $[t-1,t+h]$, keeping the lower endpoint fixed. Boundedness of $u^\beta$
and $F_\beta$ gives, for $t\ge1$ and $0<h\le1$,
\begin{equation}\label{small:uniform-time-modulus}
 \begin{split}
 \|u^\beta(t+h)-u^\beta(t)\|_\infty
 &\le Ch+C\int_0^1\min\{1,h/r\}\,dr\\
 &\le Ch(1+|\log h|)\le C_\theta h^\theta,
 \qquad 0<\theta<1.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The Lipschitz continuity of $f$ gives the same temporal modulus for
$F_\beta$. To differentiate at time $t\ge2$, again treat $t-1$ as a fixed
starting time and subtract the terminal reaction value. The resulting
cancellation is
\begin{equation}\label{small:time-cancellation}
 \begin{split}
 u_t^\beta(t)={}&(\partial_r\mathsf S_\beta)(1)u^\beta(t-1)
              +\mathsf S_\beta(1)F_\beta(t)\\
 &+\int_0^1(\partial_r\mathsf S_\beta)(r)
       [F_\beta(t-r)-F_\beta(t)]\,dr.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The last integrand has norm at most $Cr^{\theta-1}$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{small:uniform-time-derivative}
 \sup_{0<\beta\le\beta_*}\sup_{t\ge2}
       \|u_t^\beta(t)\|_\infty\le C.
\end{equation}
These estimates use the invariant bound $0\le u^\beta\le1$ and the boundedness
and Lipschitz continuity of $f$ on $[0,1]$. They require neither spatial
regularity of the initial datum nor concavity.

For each fixed $\beta$, the positive-time differences
$(u^\beta(t+h)-u^\beta(t))/h$ satisfy the same homogeneous interface law,
with reaction coefficient
$\int_0^1f'((1-\theta)u^\beta(t)+\theta u^\beta(t+h))\,d\theta$.
Passing to the limit at positive times yields the linear evolution for
$v_\beta=u_t^\beta$:
\[
 (v_\beta)_t=(v_\beta)_{xx}+f'(u^\beta)v_\beta,\qquad
 [v_\beta]=\beta(v_\beta)_x(t,0^\pm),\qquad [(v_\beta)_x]=0.
\]
The identities hold first in the mild sense on intervals separated from
zero; fixed-parameter parabolic regularity with $f\in C^2$ then gives the
one-sided traces. This regularity is used only to justify the equation and
boundary identities. Since $f'(u^\beta)\le-a_*$ on the outer moving interval,
$\Psi$ from~\eqref{small:saturation-screen} is also a supersolution for
$\partial_t-\partial_{xx}-f'(u^\beta)$ there. Compare both $v_\beta$ and
$-v_\beta$ with $\Psi$. The common global bound
in~\eqref{small:uniform-time-derivative} controls the initial data and
lateral endpoints. Thus, after increasing the common starting time,
\begin{equation}\label{small:inner-time-decay}
 |u_t^\beta(t,x)|\le Ce^{-\omega t},\qquad |x|\le c_{\rm in}t.
\end{equation}
The constants are obtained by comparison and do not depend on a
boundary regularity estimate as $\beta\downarrow0$.

We next control the Robin traces directly. Let $k=2/\beta$, let
$\mathsf T_k(s)$ be the half-line heat operator with condition
$v_x(0)=kv(0)$, and denote its kernel by $K_k$. The
formula~\eqref{order:robin-kernel} and integration by parts give
\begin{equation}\label{small:robin-trace-kernel}
 kK_k(s,0,y)=-2k\int_0^\infty e^{-kr}G'_s(y+r)\,dr\ge0,
 \qquad
 \int_0^\infty kK_k(s,0,y)\,dy\le\frac1{\sqrt{\pi s}}.
\end{equation}
More precisely, for every $R\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{small:robin-trace-tail}
 \int_R^\infty kK_k(s,0,y)\,dy
 =2k\int_0^\infty e^{-kr}G_s(R+r)\,dr
 \le\frac{e^{-R^2/(4s)}}{\sqrt{\pi s}}.
\end{equation}
Here $ke^{-kr}\,dr$ is a probability measure, so the bounds are
independent of $k$.
Set
\[
 N_\beta=\frac{f(p_\beta)-f(q_\beta)}2,\qquad
 M_\beta=\frac{f'(p_\beta)(p_\beta)_t-f'(q_\beta)(q_\beta)_t}2.
\]
Time derivatives are written explicitly as $\partial_t D_\beta$; the dot in $\dot\alpha_0$ denotes the right derivative with respect to resistance.
The folded equations and their positive-time difference quotients yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (D_\beta)_t&=(D_\beta)_{xx}+N_\beta,
 & (D_\beta)_x(t,0)&=kD_\beta(t,0),\\
 (\partial_t D_\beta)_t&=(\partial_t D_\beta)_{xx}+M_\beta,
 & (\partial_t D_\beta)_x(t,0)&=k\partial_t D_\beta(t,0).
 \end{aligned}
\]
In particular, on the most recent unit time interval,
\begin{equation}\label{small:differentiated-robin-mild}
 \begin{split}
 D_\beta(t)&=\mathsf T_k(1)D_\beta(t-1)
       +\int_0^1\mathsf T_k(s)N_\beta(t-s)\,ds,\\
 \partial_t D_\beta(t)&=\mathsf T_k(1)\partial_t D_\beta(t-1)
       +\int_0^1\mathsf T_k(s)M_\beta(t-s)\,ds.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The definitions give
\[
 |N_\beta|\le\|f'\|_\infty|D_\beta|,\qquad
 |\partial_t D_\beta|+|M_\beta|
 \le C\bigl(|(p_\beta)_t|+|(q_\beta)_t|\bigr).
\]
Thus $D_\beta,N_\beta,\partial_t D_\beta,M_\beta$ are bounded by a common constant
on the half-line for sufficiently large times. Moreover,
$|D_\beta|\le((1-p_\beta)+(1-q_\beta))/2$.
By~\eqref{small:inner-saturation} and~\eqref{small:inner-time-decay}, all four
functions are bounded by $Ce^{-\omega t}$ on
$0\le y\le R_t:=c_{\rm in}(t-1)$ throughout $[t-1,t]$, once this interval
lies beyond the common decay threshold.
Multiply the boundary traces in~\eqref{small:differentiated-robin-mild}
by $k$ and split the integrals at $R_t$. Equations
\eqref{small:robin-trace-kernel}--\eqref{small:robin-trace-tail} give
\[
 \begin{split}
 k|D_\beta(t,0)|+k|\partial_t D_\beta(t,0)|
 &\le Ce^{-\omega t}\left(1+\int_0^1s^{-1/2}\,ds\right)
       +Ce^{-R_t^2/4}\\
 &\quad+C\int_0^1s^{-1/2}e^{-R_t^2/(4s)}\,ds
 \le Ce^{-\omega't}.
 \end{split}
\]
For each fixed $\beta$, the positive-time regularity used above also
permits differentiation of the boundary value $D_\beta(t,0)$ in time,
with derivative $\partial_t D_\beta(t,0)$. The Robin condition therefore gives
\[
 d_\beta(t)=-kD_\beta(t,0),\qquad
 d'_\beta(t)=-k\partial_t D_\beta(t,0).
\]
In particular $d_\beta\in C^1((0,\infty))$. The trace estimates prove
\eqref{small:flux-decay} after reducing the common decay rate if necessary;
no uniform estimate for $u_{tx}^\beta$ is needed.

label: small:negative-bulk-potential
title: Proof
body_md:
We first establish a negative potential behind the front. Choose
$\delta,a_*>0$ so that $f'(s)\le-a_*$ on $[1-\delta,1]$.
Parameter ordering and phase convergence for $\beta_*$ allow a fixed
$K_*>0$ and a common starting time such that
$q_\beta(t,x)\ge1-\delta$ for $0\le x\le m(t)-K_*$ and
$0\le\beta\le\beta_*$. Reflection comparison gives the same lower bound
for $p_\beta$ in this range.
To cover the remaining donor-side region, put $L=-a>0$, where $a$ is from
Assumption~\ref{hyp:data}, and consider the Dirichlet heat solution
\[
 v(t,y)=\int_L^\infty[G_t(y-s)-G_t(y+s)]\,ds,\qquad y>0.
\]
Its initial datum lies below $p_\beta(0,\cdot)$, its boundary value is zero,
and $f(p_\beta)\ge0$, so $p_\beta\ge v$ for every $0\le\beta\le\beta_*$.
For $y\ge L$,
\[
 1-v(t,y)=\frac12\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{y-L}{2\sqrt t}\right)
          +\frac12\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{y+L}{2\sqrt t}\right).
\]
Since $m(t)-K_*\sim2t$, this deficit is at most $Ce^{-ct}$ uniformly for
$y\ge m(t)-K_*$ at large times. Thus both $u^\beta$ and $U$ lie in
$[1-\delta,1]$ whenever $x\le m(t)-K_*$. The entire secant segment lies
in that interval, proving
\begin{equation}\label{small:negative-bulk-potential}
 c_\beta(t,x)\le-a_*\qquad(x\le m(t)-K_*),
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently large times, uniformly in $0<\beta\le\beta_*$.

Take an even $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ equal to one near zero and set
\begin{equation}\label{small:jump-lift}
 V_\beta=W_\beta-\frac12d_\beta(t)\operatorname{sgn}(x)\chi(x).
\end{equation}
By~\eqref{small:quotient-jump}, $V_\beta$ and its first spatial derivative
are continuous across zero. Its full-space equation holds in distributions:
\begin{equation}\label{small:lifted-equation}
 (V_\beta)_t=(V_\beta)_{xx}+c_\beta V_\beta+\mathcal F_\beta,
 \quad
 \mathcal F_\beta=\frac{\operatorname{sgn}(x)}2
 \bigl(d_\beta\chi''+c_\beta d_\beta\chi-d'_\beta\chi\bigr).
\end{equation}
There are no singular interface terms because the two jumps vanish.
Lemma~\ref{small:uniform-flux} gives $|\mathcal F_\beta|\le Ce^{-\omega t}$,
with support in the fixed compact set $\operatorname{supp}\chi$.

In the coordinate $z=x-m(t)$, set $r_\beta(t,z)=e^{x-2t}V_\beta(t,x)$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{small:weighted-lift-equation}
 (r_\beta)_t=(r_\beta)_{zz}-\frac3{2t}(r_\beta)_z
 -(1-c_\beta)r_\beta+e^{x-2t}\mathcal F_\beta,
\end{equation}
where the coefficients on the right are evaluated at $x=m(t)+z$.
Choose $\lambda>1$ close enough to one that
$\lambda^2<1+a_*$ and $2(\lambda-1)<\omega$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{small:psi-screen}
 \psi(z)=\begin{cases}
 e^{\lambda(z+K_*)},&z<-K_*,\\
 1+\lambda(z+K_*),&z\ge-K_*.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
For $\mathscr Q_\beta=\partial_t-\partial_{zz}
+\frac3{2t}\partial_z+(1-c_\beta)$, we have
$\mathscr Q_\beta\psi\ge0$ at large times. On the left this follows from
\eqref{small:negative-bulk-potential} and $1+a_*-\lambda^2>0$;
on the right it follows from $c_\beta\le1$ and $\psi'\ge0$.
The weight is $C^1$, so its second derivative has no measure at the join.

Choose a common $T$ large enough that these estimates hold and
$\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset(-\infty,m(t)-K_*)$ for $t\ge T$.
On the support of the forcing,
\[
 \sup_x\frac{e^{x-2t}|\mathcal F_\beta(t,x)|}{\psi(x-m(t))}
 \le C e^{-[\omega-2(\lambda-1)]t}t^{-3\lambda/2}.
\]
Accordingly, choose the same bounded increasing function for all parameters,
\[
 A(t)=A_0+C\int_T^t
 e^{-[\omega-2(\lambda-1)]s}s^{-3\lambda/2}\,ds,
\]
with $C$ large enough to dominate this forcing bound.
The Gaussian estimate~\eqref{small:finite-gaussian} and the compact support
of the lifting allow a common $A_0$ such that
$|V_\beta(T,x)|\le A_0e^{2T-x}\psi(x-m(T))$ for all $x$.
To apply comparison, return to the original variables and set
\[
 \mathcal V(t,x)=A(t)e^{2t-x}\psi(x-m(t)).
\]
Then $(\partial_t-\partial_{xx}-c_\beta)\mathcal V\ge|\mathcal F_\beta|$
in distributions. The function $\mathcal V$ is bounded on each strip
$[T,T_1]\times\mathbb R$, $T_1>T$: as $x\to-\infty$ it decays like
$e^{(\lambda-1)x}$, and as $x\to+\infty$ like a linear factor times $e^{-x}$.
The same boundedness holds uniformly in $\beta$ for $V_\beta$ by
\eqref{small:finite-quotient-bound} and~\eqref{small:flux-decay}.
Although $c_\beta$ may jump at zero, it is a bounded measurable coefficient
on the full line. The convex approximation used in the proof of
Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-amplitudes}, now including the source, gives
\[
 (\partial_t-\partial_{xx}-c_\beta)|V_\beta|\le|\mathcal F_\beta|
\]
in distributions. The approximation is valid across zero because
$V_\beta$ and $(V_\beta)_x$ are continuous there, so no interface measure
is generated. To justify full-space comparison, set
$Z=|V_\beta|-\mathcal V$ and apply the positive-part version of the same
inequality. With $M=\|c_\beta\|_\infty\le\|f'\|_\infty$, heat-kernel
testing of the bounded distributional subsolution gives
\[
 \|Z_+(t)\|_\infty\le M\int_T^t\|Z_+(s)\|_\infty\,ds,
 \qquad Z_+(T)=0.
\]
The testing can be performed first with smooth spatial cutoffs and then
on the whole line; boundedness permits removal of the cutoffs against the
Gaussian kernel. Gronwall's inequality yields $Z_+=0$, hence
$|V_\beta|\le\mathcal V$. Since $A$ is uniformly bounded,
\begin{equation}\label{small:weighted-quotient-screen}
 |r_\beta(t,z)|\le C\psi(z).
\end{equation}

We now check the hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-amplitudes}.
Choose a common $T_0\ge T$ large enough that $x=m(t)-t^\rho$ lies to the
right of $\operatorname{supp}\chi$ and $-t^\rho<-K_*$ for $t\ge T_0$.
At this negative cutoff, $V_\beta=W_\beta$ and the normalized trace satisfies
\[
 |Z_{W_\beta}(\log t,0)|
 =|t e^{x-2t}W_\beta(t,x)|
 \le Ct e^{-\lambda t^\rho}
 \le C e^{-(\lambda/2)t^\rho}.
\]
The equality uses $m(t)=2t-\frac32\log t$.
At the fixed time $T_0$,~\eqref{small:finite-gaussian} supplies the common
$X_{1/5}$ bound for $Z_{W_\beta}(\log T_0,\cdot)$ established in the first
subsection. The solutions $W_\beta$ are classical on the right half-line,
continuous up to $T_0$, and uniformly bounded on every finite time strip.
Their coefficients are continuous there, and concavity and $f'(0)=1$ give
\[
 c_\beta\le1,\qquad
 0\le1-c_\beta\le C(u^\beta+U).
\]
With the cutoff $\chi$ fixed once and for all, the quantities
$K_*,\lambda,T,T_0$ and the constants in these bounds can all be chosen
in terms of $f,u_0,\beta_*,\rho$, independently of
$\beta\in(0,\beta_*]$. Thus all hypotheses of the corollary hold with
common constants and with the two background solutions $u^\beta,u^0$.
It yields signed amplitudes $\alpha_{W_\beta}$ and a common moment error.
For each fixed $\beta>0$, linearity of the moment and
Lemma~\ref{lem:leading-edge} identify
\[
 \alpha_{W_\beta}=\frac{\alpha_\beta-\alpha_0}{\beta}.
\]
Substituting this identity in~\eqref{front:signed-moment} proves
\eqref{small:moment-uniform-error}.

label: small:response-moment-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $0<\rho<1/3$. For each fixed, sufficiently large $t$, finite-time
convergence from Proposition~\ref{small:finite-variation} and the common
Gaussian bound~\eqref{small:finite-gaussian} permit dominated convergence:
\[
 \frac{\mathcal J_\beta(t)-\mathcal J_0(t)}\beta
 \longrightarrow
 \mathcal J_w(t):=e^{-2t}\int_{\ell(t)}^\infty
 (x-\ell(t))e^xw(t,x)\,dx
 \qquad(\beta\downarrow0).
\]
At one fixed such time, Lemma~\ref{small:scaled-moment} therefore bounds
$(\alpha_\beta-\alpha_0)/\beta$ for small $\beta$.
Applying its uniform error estimate at any sufficiently large $t$ gives
\[
 2\sqrt\pi\left(
 \limsup_{\beta\downarrow0}\frac{\alpha_\beta-\alpha_0}{\beta}
 -\liminf_{\beta\downarrow0}\frac{\alpha_\beta-\alpha_0}{\beta}\right)
 \le 2Ct^{\rho-1/2}.
\]
Letting $t\to\infty$ shows that the two finite limits coincide, proving
existence of $\dot\alpha_0$. Passing $\beta\downarrow0$ in the same estimate
now yields the quantitative bound
\begin{equation}\label{small:response-moment-bound}
 |\mathcal J_w(t)-2\sqrt\pi\dot\alpha_0|\le Ct^{\rho-1/2}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{small:response-moment-limit}
 \dot\alpha_0=\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathcal J_w(t).
\end{equation}

The moment $\mathcal J_w$ uses the fixed cutoff exponent $\rho$, but
\eqref{small:response-moment-limit} identifies its limiting amplitude with
the same derivative $\dot\alpha_0$ for every $0<\rho<1/3$.
The common negative-cutoff trace bound passes to $w$ by pointwise
convergence at each fixed time. At $T_0$, the common Gaussian bound
\eqref{small:finite-gaussian} passes to $w$ as well and gives the initial
$X_{1/5}$ estimate: equivalently, take the pointwise limit in the common
weighted bound for $Z_{W_\beta}$ and then the supremum over $y\ge0$.
Its equation has coefficient $f'(U)$, which is continuous, bounded, and satisfies
\[
 f'(U)\le1,\qquad 0\le1-f'(U)\le\|f''\|_\infty U.
\]
Together with the regularity and finite-strip boundedness from
Proposition~\ref{small:finite-variation}, these verify the hypotheses of
Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-amplitudes} for $w$, using $u^0$ as both background
solutions. The corollary gives an amplitude $\alpha_w$;
\eqref{small:response-moment-limit} identifies it as $\dot\alpha_0$.
For any fixed $0<\theta<1/3$, choose $0<\rho<\theta$ and use
\eqref{front:signed-intermediate} to obtain~\eqref{small:response-amplitude}.
Finally, substituting $\alpha_\beta=\alpha_0+\beta\dot\alpha_0+o(\beta)$
into~\eqref{order:tau-alpha} proves~\eqref{small:delay-expansion}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:reflection-comparison} gives $U_x(t,0)<0$ for $t>0$.
The positive-semigroup argument in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:pointwise-order}, now with Neumann and Dirichlet
semigroups and nonnegative Dirichlet input, gives $R,H\ge0$ in
\eqref{small:cooperative-response}; the positive
Dirichlet boundary value of $H$ and the strong maximum principle give
$H(t,x)>0$ for $t>0,x>0$.
For each fixed $s>0$, the initial end states and the full-line comparisons
\[
 0\le1-U(s,\cdot)\le G_s*(1-u_0),\qquad
 0\le U(s,\cdot)\le e^sG_s*u_0
\]
give $p(s,x)\to1$ and $q(s,x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$.
The first comparison uses $f(U)\ge0$, and the second uses $f(U)\le U$.
Since $f'(1)<f'(0)$, we have
$B(s,x)>0$ for sufficiently large $x$. Continuity therefore makes $BH$
strictly positive on a nonempty space-time open set before any prescribed
time $t>0$.
Choose $L\ge\|A\|_\infty$ and write
$R_t=R_{xx}-LR+(A+L)R+BH$. The Neumann heat kernel is strictly positive,
including at its boundary argument. Its Duhamel representation, with
nonnegative sources $(A+L)R$ and $BH$, thus gives $R(t,0)>0$ for every
$t>0$. This argument uses concavity, but does not require strict concavity.

On the right half-line, $-w=R+H$, and
\eqref{small:cooperative-response} shows that $R+H$ solves the scalar
linear equation with potential $A+B=f'(q)=f'(U)$.
The function $k=-U_x/2$ solves the same equation and has boundary value
$-U_x(t,0)/2$. To justify its zero initial datum despite the possible
roughness of $u_0$, recall that $u_0=0$ on $[b,\infty)$ for some $b<0$.
Differentiating the full-line heat representation of $U$ gives, with
$d=-b>0$,
\[
 \|U_x(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty(0,\infty)}
 \le Ct^{-1/2}e^{-d^2/(4t)}+C\sqrt t
 \longrightarrow0\qquad(t\downarrow0).
\]
Here the first term bounds the initial heat evolution on the right
half-line, and the second uses boundedness of $f(U)$ and
$\|G'_r\|_{L^1}\le Cr^{-1/2}$.
Consequently, $R+H-k$ is bounded on finite time strips, has zero initial
datum uniformly, and has boundary value $R(t,0)$. Uniqueness for
\eqref{small:positive-correction} identifies
\begin{equation}\label{small:variation-decomposition}
 Z=R+H-k,\qquad w=\frac12U_x-Z.
\end{equation}
This also constructs the solution $Z$ in the stated class. Comparison
and the strong maximum principle, using $R(t,0)>0$, give $Z(t,x)>0$
for all $t>0,x>0$.

The gradient limit in~\eqref{front:intermediate}, with $\beta=0$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{small:background-gradient}
 \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{e^{t^\theta}U_x(t,m(t)+t^\theta)}{t^\theta}=-\alpha_0
 \qquad(0<\theta<1/3).
\end{equation}
Combining this with~\eqref{small:response-amplitude} and
\eqref{small:variation-decomposition} proves that the limit
in~\eqref{small:zeta-definition} exists and equals
$-\alpha_0/2-\dot\alpha_0$, independently of $\theta$.
To prove that it is strictly positive, we apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:positive-tail} directly to $Z$. The solution is positive,
classical, and bounded on every finite time strip away from $t=0$,
and its coefficient $f'(U)$ is bounded. Moreover,
\eqref{eq:uniform-leading-bound} and $f\in C^2([0,1])$ imply, for all
sufficiently large $t$ and $z\ge0$,
\[
 U(t,m(t)+z)\le Ct e^{-z},\qquad
 f'(U(t,m(t)+z))\ge1-\|f''\|_\infty U(t,m(t)+z)
 \ge1-Ct e^{-z}.
\]
All hypotheses of the lemma hold, so the lower limit of the normalized
$Z$ in~\eqref{small:zeta-definition} is strictly positive. Since its limit
already exists, $\zeta>0$. Substitution into
\eqref{small:delay-expansion} proves~\eqref{small:coefficient-formula}.

title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall the Neumann heat semigroup $\mathsf N(t)$ on the half-line and put
\[
 b_\beta(t,x)=2\int_0^tG_{t-s}(x)j_\beta(s)\,ds.
\]
The mild formulas with boundary loss and input give
\[
 \begin{split}
 p_N(t)-p_\beta(t)
 &=b_\beta(t)+\int_0^t\mathsf N(t-s)
       [f(p_N(s))-f(p_\beta(s))]\,ds,\\
 q_\beta(t)&=b_\beta(t)+\int_0^t\mathsf N(t-s)f(q_\beta(s))\,ds.
 \end{split}
\]
Since $\|b_\beta(t)\|_\infty\le2\varepsilon\sqrt{t/\pi}$,
contractivity of $\mathsf N$ and the Lipschitz continuity of $f$, with
$f(0)=0$, imply
\[
 \mathcal E_\beta(t):=\|p_N(t)-p_\beta(t)\|_\infty+\|q_\beta(t)\|_\infty
 \le C\varepsilon\sqrt t+\|f'\|_\infty\int_0^t \mathcal E_\beta(s)\,ds.
\]
Gronwall's inequality proves~\eqref{large:finite-time}.
These formulas hold up to the boundary for positive times. The initial
profiles vanish near the interface, so the heat representations also give
$p_\beta(t,0),q_\beta(t,0),h(t)\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$.
Thus $j_\beta$ has the stated continuous extension at zero. The identity
$j_\beta/\varepsilon=p_\beta(t,0)-q_\beta(t,0)$ now gives
\[
 \sup_{0\le t\le T}
 \left|\frac{j_\beta(t)}\varepsilon-h(t)\right|\le C_T\varepsilon.
\]

Writing $f(q)=q-g(q)$, the receiving-side formula becomes
\[
 q_\beta(t,x)=2\int_0^t e^{t-s}G_{t-s}(x)j_\beta(s)\,ds
 -\int_0^t e^{t-s}
      \bigl[\mathsf N(t-s)g(q_\beta(s))\bigr](x)\,ds.
\]
By~\eqref{eq:g} and~\eqref{large:finite-time},
$\sup_{s\le T}\|g(q_\beta(s))\|_\infty\le C_T\varepsilon^2$.
Divide the formula by $\varepsilon$ and subtract $v(t,x)$.
The flux error contributes at most
$C_T\varepsilon\int_0^t(t-s)^{-1/2}\,ds$, and the nonlinear term
contributes at most $C_T\varepsilon\int_0^t e^{t-s}\,ds$.
This proves~\eqref{large:linear-input-error} and hence~\eqref{large:seed}.

Continuity and positivity of $v_T$ follow from its integral representation,
$h(s)>0$ for $s>0$, and the integrable bound $G_r(x)\le Cr^{-1/2}$.
After even extension, Tonelli's theorem and
$\int_\mathbb R e^xG_r(x)\,dx=e^r$ give
\[
 e^{-2T}\int_\mathbb R e^xv_T(x)\,dx
 =2e^{-2T}\int_0^T e^{2(T-s)}h(s)\,ds=2I_T,
\]
which proves~\eqref{large:seed-mass}.

label: large:small-data
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{large:small-data}
Let $\chi\in C_c(\mathbb R)$ be fixed, nonzero, and nonnegative. For
$\delta>0$ small enough that $\delta\|\chi\|_\infty\le1$, let $v^\delta$
solve the full-line problem
\[
 v_t=v_{xx}+v-v^2,\qquad v(0,x)=\delta\chi(x).
\]
Normalize the minimal-speed logistic wave by
$U_{\rm log}(z)\sim ze^{-z}$ as $z\to+\infty$. This fixes its tail coefficient at one, rather than imposing $U_{\rm log}(0)=1/2$. Denote the displacement parameter of the right-moving front by $x_\delta$, using the sign convention of~\cite{MRR2022}, so that
\[
 v^\delta(t,m(t)+z)\longrightarrow U_{\rm log}(z+x_\delta)
 \qquad(t\to\infty)
\]
locally uniformly in $z$. In the phase convention $U(z-\xi)$ used above, the corresponding phase is $\xi_{{\rm log},\delta}=-x_\delta$. Define its leading-edge amplitude to be the tail coefficient of this limiting profile,
$\alpha_{\rm log}(\delta\chi):=e^{-x_\delta}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{large:small-data-amplitude}
 \alpha_{\rm log}(\delta\chi)
 \sim\frac{\delta\log\delta^{-1}}{2\sqrt\pi}
 \int_\mathbb R e^x\chi(x)\,dx\qquad(\delta\downarrow0).
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
With this wave normalization and sign convention for the shift,
Mytnik--Roquejoffre--Ryzhik~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{MRR2022} give
\[
 x_\delta=\log\delta^{-1}-\log\log\delta^{-1}
 -\log\left(\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}\int_\mathbb R e^x\chi(x)\,dx\right)+o(1).
\]
Our fixed, nonnegative, continuous, compactly supported profile satisfies
their hypotheses. Exponentiating the negative of this expansion proves
\eqref{large:small-data-amplitude}.

label: large:lower-comparison
title: Proof
body_md:
By~\eqref{eq:g}, choose $C_f\ge1$, depending only on $f$, such that
$f(s)\ge s-C_fs^2$ on $[0,1]$.
Fix $T>0$ and choose a nonzero, nonnegative, even function
$\chi\in C_c(\mathbb R)$ such that, for some $0<\eta<1$,
\[
 \chi(x)\le(1-\eta)v_T(x)\qquad(x\in\operatorname{supp}\chi),
\]
where $v_T$ is extended evenly. Since $v_T$ is continuous and strictly
positive, the gap $v_T-\chi$ on this compact support is at least
$\eta\min_{\operatorname{supp}\chi}v_T>0$.
The uniform convergence in~\eqref{large:seed} therefore gives
$\varepsilon\chi\le q_\beta(T)$ on $x\ge0$ for all sufficiently small
$\varepsilon$, with the threshold allowed to depend on $T,\chi,\eta$.
Outside the support this comparison follows from $q_\beta\ge0$.
Let $w^\varepsilon$ solve the full-line problem
\[
 w_t=w_{xx}+w-C_fw^2,\qquad w(0,x)=\varepsilon\chi(x).
\]
Further restrict $\varepsilon$ so that
$\varepsilon\|\chi\|_\infty\le1/C_f$. Comparison with the constant
solutions gives
\[
 0\le w^\varepsilon(t,x)\le1/C_f\le1\qquad(t\ge0,x\in\mathbb R).
\]
Hence $w^\varepsilon_t-w^\varepsilon_{xx}
=w^\varepsilon-C_f(w^\varepsilon)^2\le f(w^\varepsilon)$ throughout
its evolution. Evenness and uniqueness imply
$w^\varepsilon_x(s,0)=0$ for $s>0$, whereas
\[
 -w^\varepsilon_x(s,0)=0\le j_\beta(T+s)
 =-q_{\beta,x}(T+s,0).
\]
The half-line comparison principle, with the initial ordering at time $T$,
therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{large:lower-comparison}
 q_\beta(t,x)\ge w^\varepsilon(t-T,x)\qquad(t\ge T,x\ge0).
\end{equation}

The function $C_fw^\varepsilon$ solves the standard logistic equation
with initial datum $C_f\varepsilon\chi$. Write
$x_\varepsilon^{\rm log}$ for its displacement parameter in the convention $U_{\rm log}(z+x_\varepsilon^{\rm log})$ of Lemma~\ref{large:small-data}, and define
\[
 \alpha[w^\varepsilon]
 :=C_f^{-1}e^{-x_\varepsilon^{\rm log}}
 =C_f^{-1}\alpha_{\rm log}(C_f\varepsilon\chi).
\]
Lemma~\ref{large:small-data}, applied with $\delta=C_f\varepsilon$, gives
\[
 \alpha[w^\varepsilon]
 \sim\frac{\varepsilon\log\varepsilon^{-1}}{2\sqrt\pi}
       \int_\mathbb R e^x\chi(x)\,dx.
\]
Indeed, the multiplicative $C_f$ cancels, and
$\log(C_f\varepsilon)^{-1}
=\log\varepsilon^{-1}-\log C_f\sim\log\varepsilon^{-1}$.

For fixed $\varepsilon,T,\chi$, evaluate~\eqref{large:lower-comparison}
at $x=m(t)+z$. Since
\[
 x-m(t-T)=z+m(t)-m(t-T)=z+2T+o(1),
\]
phase convergence for the actual solution and for the logistic comparison
solution gives, for every fixed $z\in\mathbb R$,
\[
 U_*(z-\xi_\beta)
 \ge C_f^{-1}U_{\rm log}(z+2T+x_\varepsilon^{\rm log}).
\]
Now let $z\to+\infty$. The coefficient of $ze^{-z}$ on the left is
$\alpha_\beta$, and that on the right is
$e^{-2T}\alpha[w^\varepsilon]$. Thus
\[
 \alpha_\beta\ge e^{-2T}\alpha[w^\varepsilon].
\]
This comparison uses the tails of the two limiting waves and does not
require their profiles to coincide. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$
with $T,\chi$ fixed gives
\begin{equation}\label{large:truncated-lower-bound}
 \liminf_{\beta\to\infty}\frac{\beta\alpha_\beta}{\log\beta}
 \ge\frac{e^{-2T}}{2\sqrt\pi}\int_\mathbb R e^x\chi(x)\,dx.
\end{equation}

To recover the full profile, choose continuous even cutoffs
$0\le\eta_n\le1$ with compact support, $\eta_n=1$ on $[-n,n]$,
and $\eta_n\uparrow1$ pointwise. For $n\ge2$, set
\[
 \chi_n=(1-1/n)\eta_n v_T.
\]
Each $\chi_n$ is admissible with gap parameter $\eta=1/n$, and
$\chi_n\uparrow v_T$. Apply~\eqref{large:truncated-lower-bound} first
for each fixed $T,n$, and then let $n\to\infty$.
Monotone convergence and~\eqref{large:seed-mass} yield
\[
 \liminf_{\beta\to\infty}\frac{\beta\alpha_\beta}{\log\beta}
 \ge\frac{I_T}{\sqrt\pi}.
\]
No uniform small-data asymptotics in $n$ or $T$ are required: the
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$ limit was taken with both fixed.
Finally, $I_T\uparrow I$ as $T\to\infty$, proving
\begin{equation}\label{large:lower-limit}
 \liminf_{\beta\to\infty}\frac{\beta\alpha_\beta}{\log\beta}
 \ge\frac I{\sqrt\pi}.
\end{equation}

label: large:moment-bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{large:moment-bound}
Under Assumptions~\ref{hyp:f}--\ref{hyp:data}, let $\beta\ge e^2$ and
use the rescaling and weight above. The moment
\[
 \mathcal M(\sigma)=\int_0^\infty W(\sigma,\eta)r(\sigma,\eta)\,d\eta
\]
is finite and locally absolutely continuous for $\sigma\ge0$, with
$\mathcal M(0)=0$. There is a constant $C$, depending only on $f,u_0$,
such that, for all $\sigma\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{large:uniform-first-moment}
 \int_0^\infty\eta r(\sigma,\eta)\,d\eta
 \le\mathcal M(\sigma)\le2IL+C\log(2+L)+C.
\end{equation}
head: environment

label: large:mass-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
We first bound the mass and boundary trace. Full-space linear comparison
in~\eqref{large:point-source} gives
\[
 Q_\beta(t,X)\le2\int_0^t e^{t-s}G_{t-s}(X)j_\beta(s)\,ds.
\]
Changing variables in the mass integral, enlarging its spatial domain to
$\mathbb R$, and using $\int_\mathbb R e^XG_r(X)\,dX=e^r$ yield
\begin{equation}\label{large:mass-bound}
 \int_0^\infty r(\sigma,\eta)\,d\eta
 \le 2\sqrt{1+t}\int_0^t\frac{j_\beta(s)}\varepsilon e^{-2s}\,ds
 \le2I e^{\sigma/2}.
\end{equation}
For $b(\sigma)=r(\sigma,0)$,~\eqref{large:linear-bound} implies
$b\le C\varepsilon e^t/(1+t)\le Ce^{-3L/4}$ when $t\le L/4$.
For $t\ge L/4$, the bound $Q_\beta\le1$ gives
$b\le(1+t)^{-1/2}$. Since $d\sigma=dt/(1+t)$,
\begin{equation}\label{large:boundary-bound}
 \int_0^\infty b(\sigma)\,d\sigma
 \le Ce^{-3L/4}\log(1+L)+CL^{-1/2}\le CL^{-1/2}.
\end{equation}

Define the source weight without evaluating $W$ at negative arguments:
\[
 \mathcal W_s(\sigma)=
 \begin{cases}
 W(\sigma,\eta_s(t)),&\eta_s(t)>0,\\
 0,&\eta_s(t)\le0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad t=e^\sigma-1.
\]
Using~\eqref{large:adjoint-residual} and $W(\sigma,0)=0$, integration
by parts gives, for almost every $\sigma>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{large:moment-identity}
 \begin{split}
 \mathcal M'={}&W_\eta(\sigma,0)b(\sigma)
 +k^2e^{-\sigma}\int_0^\infty\psi' r\,d\eta
 -\int_0^\infty WN\,d\eta\\
 &+2\frac{j_\beta(t)}\varepsilon(1+t)^{3/2}e^{-2t}
 \mathcal W_s(\sigma).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
We justify this identity in its time-integrated form. First fix $\beta$
and a finite physical time horizon $T$. The linear Gaussian bound and
$j_\beta\le\varepsilon$ give
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}(1+|X|)e^X Q_\beta(t,X)\,dX
 \le C_T\varepsilon t,\qquad 0\le t\le T,
\]
because $\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|X|)e^XG_s(X)\,dX$ is bounded for
$0<s\le T$. On $\eta\ge0$, we have $W\le C(1+\eta)$, and the
coordinate change therefore implies
\[
 0\le\mathcal M(\log(1+t))\le C_{\beta,T}t\longrightarrow0
 \qquad(t\downarrow0).
\]
This establishes the initial weighted trace. These finite-time constants
are used only to justify the identity, not to obtain its uniform upper bound.

Choose $\vartheta\in C_c^\infty([0,\infty))$ with
$0\le\vartheta\le1$, $\vartheta=1$ on $[0,1]$, and $\vartheta=0$ on
$[2,\infty)$, and put $\vartheta_R(\eta)=\vartheta(\eta/R)$.
Use $W\vartheta_R$ as a spatial test function, together with a smooth
time test function, in~\eqref{large:r-equation}. Its value at zero
vanishes and its derivative there equals $W_\eta(\sigma,0)$, giving
the displayed boundary term. The distributional source gives its weight
$\mathcal W_s$ once $R$ exceeds the source position on the time interval.
All spatial derivatives can be transferred to the test function. Thus
the cutoff errors involve only $r$ multiplied by derivatives of
$W\vartheta_R$, supported in $R\le\eta\le2R$. The Gaussian bound
controls these terms on the fixed finite time interval and makes them
vanish as $R\to\infty$; no far-field derivative estimate for $r$ is needed.
Moreover, $0\le g(Q_\beta)\le C Q_\beta$ gives $N\le C(1+t)r$, so the
weighted absorption is locally integrable by the preceding moment bound.
The boundary and source terms are also locally integrable. Passing to the
limit yields the time-integrated identity, local absolute continuity of
$\mathcal M$, and~\eqref{large:moment-identity} almost everywhere.
The initial weighted trace permits integration from $\sigma=0$.
The function $\mu$ is strictly increasing from zero, so the source crosses
$\eta=0$ once. Since $W(\sigma,0)=0$ and $r$ is continuous across the
source, the crossing produces no additional atomic term in the moment.

We now integrate~\eqref{large:moment-identity} and discard its nonpositive
absorption term. The boundary contribution satisfies
\[
 \int_0^\infty W_\eta(\sigma,0)b(\sigma)\,d\sigma
 \le CL^{-1/2},
\]
because $W_\eta(\sigma,0)=1+k\sqrt\pi e^{-\sigma/2}$ is bounded.
The adjoint error is integrable uniformly in $\beta$: by
\eqref{large:mass-bound} and~\eqref{large:weight-bounds},
\[
 k^2e^{-\sigma}\int_0^\infty\psi' r\,d\eta
 \le C e^{-\sigma/2},\qquad
 \int_0^\infty C e^{-\sigma/2}\,d\sigma\le C.
\]
For the source term, when $\mu(t)<L$ we have
\[
 \sqrt{1+t}\,W(\sigma,\eta_s(t))
 =L-\mu(t)+k\psi(\eta_s(t)).
\]
Its full time integral is therefore
\begin{equation}\label{large:source-moment}
 2\int_{\{t\ge0:\,\mu(t)<L\}}\frac{j_\beta(t)}\varepsilon e^{-2t}
 \left[L-\mu(t)+k\psi(\eta_s(t))\right]dt.
\end{equation}
Here $\mu(t)\ge0$ and $0\le\eta_s(t)\le L$ on the integration region.
Using $j_\beta/\varepsilon\le h$ and~\eqref{large:weight-bounds}, the
contribution of $L-\mu(t)$ is at most $2IL$, and that of the correction
is at most $CI\log(2+L)$. Thus~\eqref{large:source-moment} is bounded by
$2IL+C\log(2+L)$.
All three retained contributions are nonnegative, so their full time
integrals bound their integrals up to any $\sigma$. Together with
$\mathcal M(0)=0$ and $W\ge\eta$, these estimates prove
\eqref{large:uniform-first-moment}.

label: large:upper-limit
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\beta\ge e^2$, so that $L$ is fixed, and take $t\to\infty$ first.
For every fixed $\eta>0$, set
\[
 \widehat\eta_t
 =\frac{\mu(t)-L+\eta\sqrt{1+t}-m(t)}{\sqrt t}
 \longrightarrow\eta.
\]
Since $\mu(t)-m(t)\to0$, the point
$X=\mu(t)-L+\eta\sqrt{1+t}$ is eventually positive. The normalized
solution $w_\beta$ from Section~\ref{front:section} satisfies the exact
relation
\[
 r(\sigma,\eta)=\beta\frac{1+t}{t}
 w_\beta(\log t,\widehat\eta_t).
\]
The profile estimate~\eqref{front:nonlinear-profile}, applied near the
positive limit $\eta$, therefore gives
\[
 r(\sigma,\eta)\longrightarrow
 \beta\alpha_\beta\eta e^{-\eta^2/4}.
\]
Apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions $\eta r(\sigma,\eta)$.
Since $\int_0^\infty\eta^2e^{-\eta^2/4}\,d\eta=2\sqrt\pi$,
Lemma~\ref{large:moment-bound} yields
\[
 2\sqrt\pi\,\beta\alpha_\beta
 \le\liminf_{\sigma\to\infty}\int_0^\infty\eta r(\sigma,\eta)\,d\eta
 \le2IL+C\log(2+L)+C.
\]
Only now divide by $L=\log\beta$ and let $\beta\to\infty$. We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{large:upper-limit}
 \limsup_{\beta\to\infty}\frac{\beta\alpha_\beta}{\log\beta}
 \le\frac I{\sqrt\pi}.
\end{equation}
The lower bound~\eqref{large:lower-limit} and this upper bound prove
\eqref{eq:large-amplitude}. Finally, the amplitude--delay relation
\eqref{order:tau-alpha} gives
\[
 \tau_\beta=\frac12\log\frac{\alpha_0}{\alpha_\beta}
 =\frac12\log\beta-\frac12\log\log\beta
 +\frac12\log\frac{\sqrt\pi\alpha_0}{I}+o(1),
\]
which is~\eqref{eq:large-delay} and completes the proof.
